schools.summary: Gill tracks the sequence of the report and has the king refuse even to see his generals.
Henry brings two counts against the mourning, that David proclaimed it and that he prolonged it.
Clarke takes the covered face and repeated name for the customary forms of grief, and Wesley reads the soldiers' stealth as fear of an evil eye.
Keil and Delitzsch make the sorrow the root of the chapter's later errors and note the seam between the first verse and the fifth.

debates.question: How is the king's mourning to be judged?

sides.position: Passionate and sinful sorrow, the root of what follows in the chapter
Unwise and unworthy, both in being proclaimed and in being prolonged
A customary form of lamentation, whatever its effect on the people

outliers.note: Alone in treating the lament as a conventional form, with a parallel from Virgil.

1.pericope_label: The king wept for Absalom; the victory was turned into mourning

schools.summary: Gill allows the words were advice rather than command and explains the liberty by a general's standing.
Clarke calls the speech insolent and sensible at once, by a good soldier who was a bad man, and Wesley glosses the shaming as disappointed hopes of reward.
Keil and Delitzsch hold Joab bound to expostulate, and Ellicott finds his whole character in the scene.

sides.position: He was bound to make it, in the king's own interest
Necessary and sensible, but far past the reverence a subject owes
Advice rather than command, excused by a general's standing in those times

outliers.note: Alone in denying that the oath threatened a revolt, reading it as language meant only to startle.

5.pericope_label: Thou hast shamed the faces of all thy servants; the king sat in the gate

schools.summary: Gill has every tribe but Judah reproving its neighbours for the rebellion and for the delay.
Henry explains why the king waited to be fetched, and suspects the strife was over whose fault the delay was.
Wesley has them quarrelling over who were authors and who abettors, with David's merits revived in their memories.
Keil and Delitzsch trace the movement to a consciousness of having wronged the king, and Ellicott to a collapse of infatuation without leadership.

debates.question: What was the strife among the tribes about?

sides.position: Whose fault it was that nobody had yet fetched the king
Mutual reproach for the rebellion, from the sense of having wronged him
A general wish to return to allegiance, wanting organisation

outliers.note: Alone in pressing that the anointing of Absalom is mentioned nowhere else and may be only a form of speech.

9.pericope_label: All the people were at strife; why speak ye not of bringing the king back?

schools.summary: Gill reads the kinship as a promise of gentle dealing, and prefers David to Amasa as the one who bowed Judah's heart.
Clarke judges the whole policy well calculated, and Wesley sees only a king escaping Joab's bondage.
Ellicott calls the appointment rash and unjust, and Keil and Delitzsch divide the message into a wise half and an unjust one.

debates.question: Was the offer of the command to Amasa justified?

sides.position: Bold, but rash and unjust: a traitor should have been punished, not rewarded
Wise to approach his own tribe, unjust to bind himself by oath to the rebels' general
A fair chance to chastise Joab and be rid of his overbearing influence

outliers.note: Alone in commending the policy outright, as the way to draw out a doubtful tribe's confidence.

themes: ye are my bones and my flesh
11.pericope_label: Ye are my brethren, my bones and my flesh; thou shalt be captain of the host

schools.summary: Gill measures the march, explains the boat, and reports Abarbinel on how the household crossed.
Henry weighs the solemnity of the crossing and sets out the three things done to recommend the submission.
Clarke notes the first mention of a ferry boat, and Wesley the motives of both men who came to meet the king.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch fix the geography and argue that the prostration came before the king crossed.

sides.position: A boat sent on purpose for the king's family
Perhaps a bridge of boats, or men carrying the household over on their shoulders
The first mention of such a thing; perhaps a bridge or a raft

outliers.note: Alone in reporting Abarbinel's suggestion that men carried the household over on their shoulders.

15.pericope_label: Shimei the son of Gera hasted to meet king David; Ziba and his fifteen sons

schools.summary: Gill reads non-imputation as pardon in effect, and limits the pardon to death by the king's own hand.
Clarke allows that only later conduct could prove the confession, and Wesley expands the king's reply into its political reasoning.
Ellicott explains the house of Joseph, defends the phrase against an argument from date, and follows the oath to its end under Solomon.

sides.position: Fair as a pardon, but rash as an oath, since it tied the king's hands against later disloyalty
A just discharge on a real confession, which the king could hardly refuse

outliers.note: Alone in setting out at length the policy of appeasing the people that lay behind the pardon.

19.pericope_label: Let not my lord impute iniquity unto me; shall there any man be put to death this day?

schools.summary: Gill weighs the versions on the man's descent and leaves open where he came from.
Henry makes the return a day of account and states the complaint as two injuries from one servant.
Clarke and Wesley read the neglected body as proof of loyalty and a refutation of the slander.
Keil and Delitzsch defend the received text at two points, and Ellicott settles the geography and the word for beard.

debates.question: Where did Mephibosheth come from, and who met whom?

sides.position: He came down to the Jordan, and it was Jerusalem's people who came out to the king
He came from his estate, or had stayed near Jerusalem because he could not travel

outliers.note: Alone in working through and rejecting three proposed emendations of the verse.

24.pericope_label: Mephibosheth had neither dressed his feet nor trimmed his beard

schools.summary: Gill weighs two senses of the phrase about dead men and reads the renunciation as contentment.
Clarke defends the ruling as a restoration of the original arrangement, and Wesley describes the same settlement.
Keil and Delitzsch date the discovery of the slander to the enforcement of the grant, and Ellicott calls the ruling weak and unjust.

debates.question: How should the division of the estate be judged?

sides.position: A restoration of the original arrangement, with a defensible payment for real service
A halfway compromise, both weak and unjust
A settlement the owner was content to let stand

outliers.note: Alone in listing the long mourning, the servant's silence and the lameness as settling the facts.

themes: the king as an angel of God
27.pericope_label: My servant deceived me; thou shalt eat bread at my table continually

schools.summary: Gill fixes the age against the common term of life and notices that the two men meant different destinations.
Henry praises the use of a large estate and sets out the refusal as unfitness for a court's business and its pleasures.
Clarke argues from the help given at Mahanaim that the congratulations cannot be suspected.
Keil and Delitzsch render the question about remaining years, and Ellicott shows that the king's offer repays the service in its own word.

debates.question: Why did David press the invitation to Jerusalem?

sides.position: For his company and his counsel, and to repay kindness as a favour rather than a debt
To compensate such a man and to keep such a friend at hand
To return the sustenance of Mahanaim in kind, multiplied manifold

outliers.note: Alone in noting that the verb for provisioning at Mahanaim is the verb used for feeding him at Jerusalem.

themes: how long have I to live
31.pericope_label: Barzillai the Gileadite came down from Rogelim; come thou over with me

schools.summary: Gill treats the age as approximate and the request as exactly bounded.
Clarke finds both old age and an Eastern court's entertainments in the verse, and Wesley compresses the refusal to its reason.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch identify Chimham from the later charge to Solomon and limit the escort to the river.

debates.question: Who gave the blessing at the parting?

sides.position: The king blessed Barzillai, a prayer for his prosperity and perhaps prophetic
Barzillai blessed the king, and then turned home

outliers.note: Alone in reading the verse as evidence for the musical establishment of David's court.

35.pericope_label: I am this day fourscore years old; let thy servant turn back again

schools.summary: Gill gives the distance to Gilgal and makes the deputation a large one of principal men.
Henry reads the grievance as a ceremony missed and the quarrel as the fruit of pride and jealousy.
Wesley takes the half of Israel for a measure of guilt and of the encouragement they had not been given.
Keil and Delitzsch settle the text and the numbers, and Ellicott traces the jealousy through the whole history.

debates.question: Why was only half of Israel present at the crossing?

sides.position: They had no notice or no time; only neighbours and the eastern tribes could come
They came slowly because they were as guilty as Judah and had no gracious message
They arrived too late for the ceremony and took the lateness for a slight

outliers.note: Alone in tracing the quarrel to a standing jealousy that outlasted David and divided the nation later.

40.pericope_label: Why have our brethren the men of Judah stolen thee away?

schools.summary: Gill identifies the speakers on both sides of the exchange.
Clarke reads the fiercer words as the weightier ones, and Wesley as a failure of temper the king dared not check.
Keil and Delitzsch explain the arithmetic of ten tribes against one, and Ellicott rejects an addition made by the Greek.

debates.question: What does the closing note about fiercer words mean?

sides.position: The fiercer words carried more weight, having more reason behind them
A failure of temper, so hot that the king did not dare interpose
Only that the answer annoyed the other side

outliers.note: Alone in explaining why the claim says ten tribes when there were strictly eleven.

themes: have we eaten of the king's cost
42.pericope_label: We have ten parts in the king; the words of the men of Judah were fiercer
